title: Trump says he'll soon decide whether to ‘make a deal’ with Iran or ‘finish it off'
description: US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Marine One as he departs the White House for Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, en route to F
body: US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Marine One as he departs the White House for Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, en route to Fort Myers, Florida, on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, US, October 23, 2026.Evan Vucci | ReutersU.S. President Donald Trump has said he was deciding whether to "make a deal" with Iran or "finish it off" as investors weigh heightened tensions across the Middle East."Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? It's getting to be decision time," Trump said in a Fox News interview on Sunday.Mediators from Qatar, which has played a key role in efforts to negotiate an agreement between Washington and Tehran, visited Tehran on Sunday, according to Reuters. It comes as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia continued over the weekend.The last confirmed U.S. strikes on Iran were on Sept. 1. Trump previously said attacks would not resume until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Tehran says it is preparing a military response to any U.S. strikes.A potential U.S. target could be Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried site linked to Iran's nuclear program, Trump said in the Sunday interview."We can read the badge on somebody's shirt from space, okay? We know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe Mountain. We know the other three [nuclear sites] are obliterated," Trump said.Trump also repeated the claim that the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global trade and a major flashpoint in the conflict, citing that crude oil flows have returned to prewar levels.Energy prices nonetheless remain elevated amid the disruption and a global refining squeeze.Washington and Tehran have both repeatedly claimed they control the route, where overall trade flows remain severely curtailed, impacting consumer prices.A Singapore-flagged container ship sank in the strait earlier this month after being struck by an unidentified projectile and catching fire.Ali Ozmaei, chief of the Iran Revolutionary Guard navy, said earlier this month that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships.Regional powers seek Iran talksSenior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are meeting Iran's leadership in Tehran on MondayThe three countries signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in August, committing to closer defense cooperation and stipulating that an armed attack against one member would be regarded as an attack against all.It is the first meeting of the group since Houthi missiles and drones targeted sites across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh airport and an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco.Saudi Arabia last week postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference until 2027 due to security concerns after a string of fatal strikes.

schema.headline: Trump says he'll soon decide whether to ‘make a deal’ with Iran or ‘finish it off'

title: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote
description: An El Al Boeing 737-958(ER) takes off from Barcelona-El Prat Airport in Barcelona, Spain, on Aug. 27, 2025. Joan Valls | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAn ext
body: An El Al Boeing 737-958(ER) takes off from Barcelona-El Prat Airport in Barcelona, Spain, on Aug. 27, 2025. Joan Valls | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAn extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes.Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters, according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems."While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during a press conference, amid the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, in Jerusalem, March 19, 2026. Ronen Zvulun | ReutersIn Israel's first election since 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, who has served as Prime Minister for 18 years over three separate periods, is facing top challenger Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, who heads the Yashar party. Both would likely need backing from potential coalition partners in order to win. Polls are extremely tight heading into Tuesday's election. Issues like security, already a major decider for Israelis, have gotten even more contentious with the Iran war in full swing. The exemption of some ultra-Orthodox men from conscription is also causing a great divide in Israeli society, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is still working on a controversial plan that would give the governing coalition more control over the judiciary.25 October 2026, Israel, Tel Aviv: Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot addresses attendees from behind a lectern emblazoned with party slogans during an election rally. Erik Marmor | Picture Alliance | Getty Images"All elections in Israel are energetic, but because this one will have such a meaningful impact on the future of the country it has been especially hard fought," Shomer said. "This election is really about how we see our future, voter turnout will be very high."Voter turnout in 2022 was just above 70% according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. Pollsters believe it could reach as high as 87% this time. Among foreign service workers serving in embassies and consulates outside of Israel, voter turnout was 90%. According to The Central Elections Committee, that number is usually closer to 70%.In order to help those living abroad come back to cast votes, an organization called Fly & Vote was set up by the America-Israel Democracy Coalition, a U.S.-based group which was originally created in 2023 to stop the effort by Likud to reform the judicial system. While organizations and political parties are prohibited from paying for any kind of transportation for people inside or outside of Israel, Aid Coalition has found other ways to facilitate the voting. Fly & Vote, which has been funded by private donations, chartered a flight for Israelis living in Portugal and bought blocks of tickets for flights from the New York area. Anyone on the flights had to pay for their own seats. "Israelis who don't live here still have a stake in what we do, and we want to help them," said Ora Peled-Nakash, the group's co-founder. "We don't take a political position though and we don't tell anyone how to vote, we just help them cast their ballot." Travelers will also have plenty of commercial options.For decades El Al was the only Israeli airline to fly routes from the U.S. to Israel. Arkia started offering flights last year and Israir earlier this year. Legacy U.S. carriers United and Delta are also flying to Israel again after suspending flights due to the war with Iran. Germany's Lufthansa flies to Israel from Europe and British Airways is scheduled to re-start flights this week. What's more, the price is in line with what it would be during normal times, Peled-Nakash said. There were still a few seats left on El Al flights from JFK or Newark airports ranging from $1,300 to $2,500 as of Sunday, according to research from CNBC.After years of political instability that saw five elections between 2019 and 2022, Tueday's election result could help shape Israel's political, security and economic direction for years to come. But it also shows how politically divided the country has become.

schema.headline: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote

title: Trump DOJ unlawfully fired Epstein prosecutor Maurene Comey, judge rules
description: A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice's firing last year of New York federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FB
body: A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice's firing last year of New York federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was unlawful.Judge Jesse Furman, in his ruling, also granted Maurene Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay as an assistant U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York from her termination on July 16, 2025, through Dec. 20, 2025, when the judge inferred she accepted another job.The DOJ said it would appeal Furman's ruling in which the judge rejected the department's arguments that the attorney general had authority to dismiss Comey without cause. The case is in in U.S. District Court in Manhattan.Comey's lawyers, in a statement, said, "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law.""As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system,'" the lawyers said. "This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law."Before her termination, Comey was involved in a series of high-profile federal prosecutions, including ones against the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean "Diddy" Combs.Her lawsuit against the DOJ argued that her termination violated federal law and the Constitution and stemmed from President Donald Trump's longstanding animus toward her father, whom Trump had fired as FBI director in 2017.James Comey is currently under federal indictment that accuses him of threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells forming the number "86 47." His attorneys are seeking to have that case tossed out. James Comey, who denies any wrongdoing, previously had another federal indictment against him filed by the DOJ under Trump dismissed.Maurene Comey's suit said the DOJ did not give "any explanation whatsoever for terminating Ms. Comey," and, "In truth, there is no legitimate explanation.""Rather, Defendants fired Ms. Comey solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B. Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both," the suit said.Furman, in his ruling for Comey, referenced that claim, but his decision was based on other grounds.The judge rejected the DOJ's arguments that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi could remove a federal prosecutor "at will" and without cause and that current Attorney General Todd Blanche could ratify that act after the fact as he did in May as acting attorney general.Furman also rejected the DOJ's argument that even if the Civil Service Reform Act requires removal of a prosecutor for cause, an attorney general's firing of her constituted an implicit determination that she was removed "for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service.""The Court need not dwell long on Defendants' second statutory argument justifying Comey's removal," Furman said, referring to that claim. "That is because the argument borders on frivolous."The judge noted that Comey was fired despite having had excellent performance reviews."Comey's supervisors and peers consistently lauded her work, describing her as a 'brilliant lawyer and a gifted supervisor,' 'the lawyer the office turns to when legal excellence is a must,' and 'an outstanding AUSA in every respect' with 'judgment, work product, and courtroom advocacy [that are] among the finest in the country,'" Furman wrote.The DOJ admitted that Comey's termination "was not 'for cause' and was not based on herperformance," Furman noted.In addition, the judge said, the DOJ's argument that Comey's termination was lawful ignored parts of the Civil Service Reform Act, which "required that Comey be given advance written notice (subject to certain exceptions not relevant here); 'a reasonable time' to respond orally and in writing; representation; and 'a written decision and the specific reasons therefor at the earliest practicable date.'""Defendants concede, as they must, that Comey was not afforded these procedural protections," the judge said.Furman also said the DOJ all but admitted that its argument that the attorney general had power to fire Comey under Article II of the U.S. Constitution — which establishes the executive branch of government — sought "to overturn nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.""This Court, however, is bound to follow the Supreme Court's precedents unless and until the Supreme Court overturns them," Furman wrote.The DOJ, in a statement, said, "The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."That appeal would happen after Furman issues a final judgment in the case. The judge reserved judgment on Comey's claim that her firing violated her First Amendment rights. Furman gave her until Nov. 9 to file arguments on why that claim should not be dismissed as moot given his order in her favor on other grounds. CNBC has requested comment on the ruling from the White House. Comey, in a note to colleagues at the U.S. Attorney's Office after she was fired, wrote, "If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decisions of those who remain.""Fear is the tool of a tyrant, wielded to suppress independent thought. Instead of fear, let this moment fuel the fire that already burns in the heart of this place," she wrote. "A fire of righteous indignation at abuses of power. Of commitment to seek justice for victims."

schema.headline: Trump DOJ unlawfully fired Epstein prosecutor Maurene Comey, judge rules

title: Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital
description: watch nowInvesting giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager su
body: watch nowInvesting giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity. The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.  Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.  For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconApollo Global Management, YTDJohn Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever. "Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

schema.headline: Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

title: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion
description: Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and superintellig
body: Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and superintelligence.The stock was down 1.6% in morning trading after the announcement. Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares, Meta said in a statement.The tech giant will initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.The news comes as hyperscalers pour record sums into the AI infrastructure build-out. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across compute, data centers and power.Meta's planned investments will support "emerging AI opportunities" including its family of apps, its AI agent Muse and its data center business, the company said Monday.It plans to balance funding for these investments through a mix of operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, partnerships and equity capital.Meta racing to secure AI infrastructureMeta is among the major hyperscalers that are increasingly tapping debt to fund the expensive infrastructure required for the AI boom.Last week, Meta posted third-quarter results showing revenue jumped 26% year on year: $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. However, investors focused more on the tech company's negative free cash flow and its higher full-year capital expenditure forecast.It now expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. That sent Meta's shares lower on Thursday. Meta is building four "superclusters" with more than 1 gigawatt of capacity each and is on track to nearly double total infrastructure capacity in 2026 on a year-over-year basis, the company said.The decision to raise more money "reflects the eye-watering levels of investment required to keep up in the AI arms race," Ben Wood, senior partner at CCS Insight, told CNBC. "Meta offering more stock comes at a time when numerous companies, such as Google, SpaceX and soon, Anthropic, are going to the markets to raise funds."Alphabet, Google's parent company, said it would look to raise $85 billion in June. SpaceX has closed a $40 billion debt financing to purchase graphics processing units. Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering.TikTok U.S. is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity over the coming years, CNBC reported Friday.

schema.headline: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion

title: NBA enters prediction markets with Kalshi, Polymarket partnerships
description: Tari Eason #17, Amen Thompson #1 of the Houston Rockets and Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers go up for the rebound during the game during R
body: Tari Eason #17, Amen Thompson #1 of the Houston Rockets and Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers go up for the rebound during the game during Round One Game Five of the 2026 NBA Playoffs on April 29, 2026 at Crypto.Com Arena in Los Angeles, California. Adam Pantozzi | National Basketball Association | Getty ImagesThe NBA is embracing prediction markets for the first time by naming leading platforms Kalshi and Polymarket as its preferred exchanges. Through the agreements, the league said there will be "significant integrity" protections for NBA markets, including limitations on which types of event contracts can be featured and information-sharing requirements regarding suspicious trades. "Protecting the integrity of the game is our top priority," said Scott Kaufman-Ross, NBA head of media distribution and partnerships in a press release. "These partnerships represent an important step in establishing a framework that creates new opportunities to engage our fans."As part of the announcements, the league also signed a memorandum of understanding with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that asserts prediction markets are under its purview. The agreement seeks to maintain the integrity of both the NBA and event contract markets, the memo said, through exchanges of information. The NBA is the latest league to create partnerships with the booming prediction markets industry, which has seen much of its growth over the past year come from the popularity of its sports-related offerings. The NHL in October 2025 announced partnerships with both Kalshi and Polymarket, while the MLB announced a relationship with the latter company in March. Those same contracts, though, are under fire by states across the country, who argue that the offerings amount to sports betting and should be regulated by them. Platforms and the CFTC argue that event contracts are swaps, a type of derivative, and thus are regulated at the federal level. Courts across the country have delivered conflicting rulings on the issue, and many expect the Supreme Court will likely be needed to resolve the dispute. "The NBA is one of the most influential sports leagues in the world, and we're excited to work together to bring fans closer to the game," said Ari Borod, president of sports business development at Polymarket, in the press release.  As preferred exchanges, Kalshi and Polymarket get rights to use NBA intellectual property along with marketing and licensing rights. watch now"It's an exciting time for both NBA fans and Kalshi users," Adam Barrick, head of sports partnerships at Kalshi, said in the release. "The relationship we've built together reflects a shared mindset that prioritizes fan engagement, innovation and safety."The NBA's move on Monday now leaves the NFL as the outlier among major American sports leagues when it comes to prediction markets. Earlier this month, the NFL in an amicus brief to the Supreme Court said that sports-related event contracts should be regulated by the states rather than the CFTC. The league added that it's not opposed to the markets, but rather thinks they should have more guardrails.At the time, Kalshi told CNBC it had tried to work more closely with the NFL, but that the league hadn't engaged. Adam Silver, the commissioner of the NBA, though, took a different approach on the regulation question in an interview with CNBC's Contessa Brewer in early October. "From at least the NBA standpoint, we have roughly 40 different jurisdictions regulating us right now," he said. "So to have a consistent policy nationally, I think would be in our best interest."— CNBC's Jessica Golden contributed reportingDisclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: NBA enters prediction markets with Kalshi, Polymarket partnerships

title: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) at the opening bell in New York City on October 19, 2026. Angela Weiss | Afp | Getty I
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) at the opening bell in New York City on October 19, 2026. Angela Weiss | Afp | Getty ImagesA version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading. Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up. Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova,  Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff. Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies. AI trade loses steamThe ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week. Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF  are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.  Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24. Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year. Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500. Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.  Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors. Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

schema.headline: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

title: Oil ticks lower as Saudi defense minister meets with Iran's president in Tehran to de-escalate
description: watch nowCrude oil prices ticked lower Monday as Saudi Arabia's defense minister held talks with Iranian leaders in Tehran in an effort to ease simmer
body: watch nowCrude oil prices ticked lower Monday as Saudi Arabia's defense minister held talks with Iranian leaders in Tehran in an effort to ease simmering tensions between the two countries. Brent crude futures lost 91 cents to close at $115.81 a barrel after briefly topping $117 earlier in the session. U.S. West Texas Intermediate fell $1.51 to settle at $101.76. Prices have gained about 12% this month. Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman met Monday with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei.Pakistan's Army Chief of Staff Asim Munir and the head of Turkish intelligence Ibrahim Kalin also participated in the talks. Pakistan and Turkey are members of a defense pact with Saudi Arabia. The meeting in Tehran came as Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly attacked Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. Houthi strikes on civilian targets, such as airports, threaten to escalate the conflict in the Middle East. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconOil prices year-to-dateThe Houthis said Monday that they fired missiles at Saudi Arabia's international airport in Riyadh and launched drones at oil pumping stations. The Saudis have not confirmed those strikes took place. The ongoing hostilities have some investors worried about the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure and the risk of another major disruption to production, refining or export facilities.Another disruption would come as global inventory levels have fallen sharply after eight months of conflict. The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, for example, is at its lowest level since 1982. Geopolitical uncertainty has already added roughly $20 a barrel to oil prices, said Michael Alfaro, chief investment officer at Gallo Partners.I think the theme we're in right now is that uncertainty is off the charts, and if you think about the risk premium that's baked into oil right now, it's about $20 a barrel.Michael AlfaroChief Investment Officer, Gallo PartnersA substantial strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline or additional refining infrastructure could send prices sharply higher, Alfaro said. But prices jumping above $120 would also destroy demand, he said. Beyond the immediate threat to crude supplies, damage to refining infrastructure could pose a more persistent challenge to global energy markets."The real challenge is refining capacity," Alfaro said, warning that the disruptions could develop into a longer-term structural problem extending into 2027 and beyond.Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia plans to begin storing crude oil in Singapore from the second half of 2027, according to energy ministers from both countries, in a move aimed at strengthening the resilience of its Asian supply chain.In the U.S., the Energy Department on Friday authorized the release of up to 400,000 barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption at a Louisiana refinery.Still, the prospect of additional supply from American producers remains uncertain, with companies reluctant to commit to major new investments amid volatile prices and geopolitical risks.Alfaro added that U.S. producers were adding some drilling rigs, but remained cautious about substantially increasing capital expenditure."We're not really seeing major capex additions to bring new rigs on or bring new production online," he said.

schema.headline: Oil ticks lower as Saudi defense minister meets with Iran's president in Tehran to de-escalate

title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: The 'cliff' beneath China's cities
description: People walk on the Bund promenade along the Huangpu River in Shanghai on January 19, 2026. Jade Gao | Afp | Getty ImagesHi, this is Anniek, writing to
body: People walk on the Bund promenade along the Huangpu River in Shanghai on January 19, 2026. Jade Gao | Afp | Getty ImagesHi, this is Anniek, writing to you from Singapore, with Evelyn, who reported from the Bund Summit in Shanghai last week. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what we are seeing and hearing from China watchers inside and outside the country.Everyone wants China to spend more. So why is its government spending less, and what happens if the most indebted cities can't afford it anymore?Governments from Washington to Brussels are being told to spend less, but Beijing is being urged to spend more. At the International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings in Bangkok earlier this month, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva called the U.S. and European countries the "worst offenders" on debt and boiled down her prescription: "China needs to spend more, the U.S. has to save more, and Europe has to invest more."Georgieva also urged Beijing to deliver more meaningful fiscal stimulus as its economy teeters on deflation, expecting China's economic growth to slow to 4.5% this year from 5% last year, and slow further to 4% in 2027. Beijing has space to borrow, with general government debt at about 68.4% of GDP, according to the IMF. But a debt crisis looms outside the government's balance sheet. The augmented government debt, including local government financing vehicles and off-balance sheet borrowing, ballooned to around 126.6% of GDP last year, IMF estimates, comparable to developed markets including the U.S. and Europe.Local authorities, for decades, relied on selling land to developers to fund development of roads, rail lines and industrial parks. That income has collapsed since the property slump began in 2021. Beijing has since moved to stop local governments from piling up new hidden debt, curbing the off-the-books borrowing, removing a key engine of growth. CF40, a Beijing think tank that co-hosted last week's Bund Summit in Shanghai, estimates that land-sale income has more than halved since 2021, to 4.2 trillion yuan, equivalent to about $590 billion, from 8.7 trillion yuan. That squeeze has fed through to spending. Combined fiscal spending declined 3.5% in the first eight months of the year, after growing 3.6% last year, Ting Lu, chief China economist at Nomura, estimates, describing it as a "true fiscal cliff" that has become a real drag on the economy. Urban fixed-asset investment declined for the first time in decades, falling 3.8% last year, and has since steepened its decline, dropping 7.2% in the first three quarters. Beijing held its official deficit target at about 4% of GDP, but the Institute of International Finance estimates the actual deficit could reach as much as 9% and says even that looks insufficient.Beijing has ordered the state-backed borrowers to clear hidden debt and transition into market-oriented commercial state-owned enterprises by mid-2027. Hidden debt in such vehicles shrank to 6.5 trillion yuan ($973.3 billion) last year from 14.3 trillion yuan in 2023, according to S&P Global Ratings. But many of the vehicles still lack the cash flow to pay interest and remain burdened with unprofitable public projects, S&P said.The IMF wants Beijing to square the circle with a medium-term fiscal framework, one that lets China "expand fiscally in the near-term [to reflate the economy] but claw back the support over the medium term so that you ensure debt sustainability," said Krishna Srinivasan, director of the fund's Asia and Pacific department. The fund also urges China to move away from point growth targets, which it says push local officials to invest excessively to hit the number, leading to resource "misallocation" and rising provincial debt.Stakes are high as letting any local government default could set a dangerous precedent. "No one wants to be the first local government official to default," said Logan Wright, partner at Rhodium Group. But once one does, and Beijing steps in, the rest can expect the same bailout, he said, meaning local officials' priorities may sometimes run counter to Beijing's. "They actually want to default." Volvo Cars CEO says China sales slump came 'faster than we thought' The Swedish automaker blamed a weaker third quarter on "tougher" market conditions in China and the U.S. CEO Håkan Samuelsson said Chinese consumers are increasingly turning to domestic brands, and the Geely-owned carmaker plans to revamp its business around "regionally adapted cars." House committee says Webull messages show China-based staff could access U.S. customer data The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party says internal Webull messages indicate employees in China could reach sensitive U.S. user data that the online brokerage had said was restricted to U.S.-based staff. The panel says that raises national security risks for American finance. Wealthy Chinese rattled by Beijing's widening tax hunt turn to the U.S. Rich Chinese are asking lawyers and bankers about opening U.S. bank accounts and moving offshore assets there, after Beijing imposed retroactive levies on offshore trusts in July. But lawyers warn that the paper trail of funds leaving CRS jurisdictions could still expose clients to retroactive taxes. schema.headline: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: The 'cliff' beneath China's cities

title: JetBlue posts bigger loss on fuel costs, but CEO says margins improving
description: JetBlue planes populate the tarmac on June 24, 2026 at JFK Airport in the Queens borough of New York City.  Bruce Bennett | Getty ImagesJetBlue Airway
body: JetBlue planes populate the tarmac on June 24, 2026 at JFK Airport in the Queens borough of New York City.  Bruce Bennett | Getty ImagesJetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but the New York carrier said strong travel demand is helping to offset higher fuel prices as it seeks to calm investors after shares fell to a new low Monday.JetBlue stock soared roughly 11% in after-hours trading Monday.JetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million. "Resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue well ahead of our initial expectations, allowing us to recapture more of the increase in fuel costs than we initially expected," CEO Joanna Geraghty said in an earnings release. "That momentum has carried into the fourth quarter, and Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver exceptional results even as we significantly grow capacity."JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.JetBlue executives are set to hold an earnings call on Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET, where they will face questions from analysts about the company's long-term health amid sustained losses. A group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday."Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:Loss per share: 60 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 55 cents expectedRevenue: $2.81 billion vs. $2.82 billion expectedJetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares, which are up more than 20% this year.JetBlue has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals. It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines, which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines.

schema.headline: JetBlue posts bigger loss on fuel costs, but CEO says margins improving

title: Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone
description: The Apple iPhone Duo smartphone at Apple's Fifth Avenue store during the first day of in-store sales in New York, US, on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. Michae
body: The Apple iPhone Duo smartphone at Apple's Fifth Avenue store during the first day of in-store sales in New York, US, on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesApple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, hit store shelves on Friday to considerable lines and long wait times for pre-orders. But some customers who were lucky enough to get the $1,999-and-up phone on its first weekend have been reporting a pretty big problem: The inner screen of the phone can break, showing horizontal bright lines emanating from the phone's hinge.Apple on Monday said it was aware of the issue, which it said affected a "small number" of phones, and that it would replace the devices under its AppleCare warranty. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," an Apple representative told CNBC. "If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."Apple says on its website that an inner-screen repair will be $999 for iPhone Duos that are out-of-warranty. Most of the reports are from anonymous customers on online forums such as Reddit and X, and there are fake images online as well. But well-respected device repair firm iFixit weighed in on Sunday, after tearing down the new device and testing its resistance to dust, and theorized the issues may have to do with Apple's hinge design."Many of these damage reports describe folding or unfolding the phone, hearing a crunch, and pushing past it," said iFixit technician Shahram Mokhtari in its teardown video. "Right where the damage is happening, the hinge is shaped a little differently.""The hinge is actually dozens of parts, with ludicrous precision," iFixit CEO Kyle Wiens posted on X. "A manufacturing variance or grain of sand can kill the fragile display panel it protects."watch nowBreaking screens have been an issue with foldable phones going back to 2019, and have been seen as one of the major roadblocks to the technology's widespread adoption. That year, Samsung released one of its first folding devices, and reviewers quickly found that its inner screen cracked during normal use. Early reviewers praised the experience of using the iPhone Duo when unfolded, especially for multitasking or media, but said that many apps had not been updated to take full advantage of the phone's larger and wider screens.Apple said on Monday that apps were already being updated for the new foldable device. "The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," an Apple representative said in a statement.

schema.headline: Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone

title: Mortgage rates above 7% are the 'new normal'—here's why
description: Everyone seems to agree that mortgage rates above 7% are the new "normal."The phrase keeps popping up lately in public comments from housing economist
body: Everyone seems to agree that mortgage rates above 7% are the new "normal."The phrase keeps popping up lately in public comments from housing economists, including Lawrence Yun, chief economist for the National Association of Realtors, and Robert Dietz, chief economist for the National Association of Home Builders. It's a sentiment increasingly reflected in forecasts, too, with major housing groups predicting mortgage rates will remain above 7% well into 2027. Fannie Mae forecasts mortgage rates could average 7.5% in 2027, while the Mortgage Bankers Association expects them to remain above 7%. That means the 3% or 4% mortgage rates borrowers were used to in the years before 2022 are unlikely to return anytime soon. "We could definitely see some movement up and down depending on data, but we're just not in the same economic environment we were in during the 2010s or the pandemic," says Jenna Stauffer, a broker and market analyst with Sotheby's International Realty.Why mortgage rates could stay higher for longerMortgage rates tend to move with the 10-year Treasury yield, which serves as a benchmark because mortgages are typically paid off or refinanced well before their 30-year term. And there are reasons to think those longer-term borrowing costs could remain elevated.One is persistently high inflation. When inflation remains elevated, investors generally demand higher yields on long-term bonds to compensate for the declining purchasing power of the money they'll eventually be repaid. Inflation, as measured by the Fed's preferred PCE price index, hasn't been below the central bank's 2% target since February 2021.But inflation isn't the only factor. The federal government is borrowing heavily, while the artificial intelligence boom is fueling enormous private investment in data centers, power generation and other infrastructure, says Selma Hepp, chief economist at real estate data firm Cotality. Together, that increased demand for capital can put upward pressure on longer-term borrowing costs, she says.Compared to the 2010s, "we've moved from a world with more capital than investment opportunities to one with tremendous competition for capital," Hepp says. Low inflation, abundant savings and relatively weak demand for capital helped keep mortgage rates low during that period, she says.Demand for mortgage bonds has weakened, too, putting upward pressure on mortgage rates. Banks have become more reluctant to hold mortgage-backed securities since the 2022-23 rate spike produced steep losses on bond portfolios, says Tom Graff, chief investment officer at wealth management firm Facet.  That's because bond prices generally fall when interest rates rise. The failures of Silicon Valley Bank and First Republic also prompted greater regulatory scrutiny of banks' bond holdings, he says.During the pandemic, the Fed pushed rates in the opposite direction. The Federal Reserve bought large quantities of Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities to push longer-term borrowing costs lower, helping drive mortgage rates to historic lows. The Fed has since stepped away from actively buying mortgage-backed securities, says Steve Kaminski, head of residential lending at TD Bank.With those low-rate conditions no longer in place, "mortgage rates will likely remain elevated for at least the next year," Kaminski says.What would it take for mortgage rates to fall?Getting mortgage rates back to around 6% would likely require lower inflation, slower economic growth or less pressure from government borrowing to help bring down the 10-year Treasury yield, Hepp says.Kaminski similarly says getting below 7% would require lower inflation and lower Treasury yields. A weakening economy could also push rates lower as investors seek the relative safety of Treasury bonds, lowering their yields, he says.Whether that happens is uncertain, which is why Hepp says she doesn't like calling 7% the "new normal," since there's nothing permanent about that particular number. But the low inflation, abundant capital and accommodative Fed policies that helped produce 3% and 4% mortgages are no longer in place, she says.For would-be homebuyers, that means waiting for significantly lower mortgage rates could be a gamble. "I don't think we should expect to return to the financial conditions that routinely produced 3% and 4% mortgages," Hepp says.

schema.headline: Mortgage rates above 7% are the 'new normal'—here's why

title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push
description: Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure
body: Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below. Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people.Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. Capital expenditures for the September quarter should exceed $50 billion, Microsoft said in July. In the same quarter a year ago, capital spending and finance leases came to $34.9 billion.That's put a strain on Microsoft's finances. In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for. Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees."The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees. "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program."Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation, increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use. It has armed programmers, sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results. At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities.The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft's financial profile. In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year.Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have decided not to participate in the new buyout, the person said. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31, the person added.More than 30% of those who could join the voluntary retirement program went ahead with it, Microsoft said in July. But that was open to those at the senior director level and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan. The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around.On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results.WATCH: Amazon, Microsoft earnings key to gauging AI investment returns: CIO

schema.headline: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push

title: Brazilian stocks rocked as Lula wins presidential election, Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede
description: SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - OCTOBER 24: Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, incumbent president of Brazil and presidential candidate for Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT)
body: SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - OCTOBER 24: Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, incumbent president of Brazil and presidential candidate for Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT) waves a Brazil flag during a rally ahead of the presidential runoff at Avenida Paulista on October 24, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil.  Alexandre Schneider | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil's president, overturning a first-round loss to beat Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The outcome triggered a sell-off in Brazilian assets as markets were caught off guard.Lula took 51.8% of valid votes to Bolsonaro's 48.2%, according to the Superior Electoral Court, with nearly all ballots counted on Sunday.The results are also historic as it's the first time since Brazil returned to direct elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the final runoff after losing in the first round.Markets jolted by Lula win Brazilian stocks plunged following the unexpected victory, unwinding some of the rally from the first-round result three weeks earlier. That reflected expectations of more market-friendly policymaking by Bolsonaro and broader jitters around Brazil's debt and spending.The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF was 25% lower at 10:30 a.m. ET, while trading on Brazil's stock exchange was halted by an automatic circuit breaker. U.S.-listed Brazilian companies also sold off. Energy giant Petrobras was last seen down 16%, banking group Itaú Unibanco fell 20%, brewer Ambev shed 10.3%, and mining firm Vale fell 1.2%. Aircraft manufacturer Embraer was 5% lower.The Brazilian real meanwhile dropped 10.5% against the U.S. dollar to its lowest level since December 2025, according to LSEG data. The Brazilian Treasury on Monday canceled auctions of inflation-linked and fixed-rate government bonds that had been scheduled for Oct. 27 and Oct. 29, saying in a notice that it would "continue to monitor market conditions and act to ensure the proper functioning of the government bond market and other related assets." An auction of Treasury Financial Bills scheduled for Oct. 27 will go ahead.Citi analysts said Monday that investors were concerned about "fiscal policy, state-owned enterprises, and the broader reform agenda" under Lula, who began his current term on Jan. 1, 2023. He was previously Brazil's president from 2003 to 2011. Banking stocks will be hit by the risk that interest rates remain higher for longer, delaying the normalization of banks' asset quality, Citi analysts also said.watch nowLula's leadership has seen mounting public debt driven by double-digit interest rates, elevated costs of servicing the debt, and rigid mandatory spending. He has pledged to extend the Bolsa Família social welfare system and reduce the working week without pay cuts."The fiscal side has always been Brazil's Achilles heel, and a 7-8% budget deficit and 70% net debt-to-GDP ratio leave Brazil vulnerable in a global bond sell-off," Chris Turner, ING's head of EMEA and Latam research, said in a note."Instead of fiscal consolidation under Bolsonaro, Brazilian assets are instead going to have to contend with Lula's campaign pledges, including a shorter working week," Turner said.Alejo Czerwonko, a fellow at the Atlantic Council, said Lula's administration will likely extend the more "gradual approach" to stabilizing its debt trajectory, building on the existing fiscal framework while seeking to preserve public investment and social spending.Goldman Sachs analysts said they expect "modest measures" to contain the government's spending growth, alongside further increases in an already high tax burden, while major structural reforms remain unlikely. Vote tensionsFinancial markets will also be monitoring how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result or "allows the constitution to run its course," ING's Turner added.Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat overnight, saying he would seek to have the result annulled, Reuters reported. He also said a ruling by a supreme court justice to extend voting for two hours was "unacceptable," according to the outlet.The election process was marred by allegations of voter suppression, with Lula's campaign reporting suspended public transportation in some key areas. Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin extended voting by two hours. Bolsonaro's campaign had also requested an extension, citing heavy rains that shut polling stations in the south, a right-wing stronghold.  Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazilian presidential candidate, speaks during a press conference at the Liberal Party (PL) camp following the runoff election in Brasilia, Brazil, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026.  Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe victory of the 80-year-old leftist, who had trailed in the first round, blocks a rightward shift in Latin America that U.S. President Donald Trump has backed. Trump called Bolsonaro's lead in the first round "a very, very big victory."He would have preferred a Brazilian president in closer alignment to U.S. foreign policy as Washington makes efforts to project U.S. power across the Americas, according to Daniela Portella Sampaio, senior research fellow for Latin American Security at the U.K. think tank Royal United Services Institute. Lula, who has publicly sparred with Trump, is set to govern from 2027 to 2030, facing a Congress where Bolsonaro's Liberal Party holds the largest bench in decades, and with a substantial public debt that he would need to stabilize. Leaders from across Latin America largely congratulated Lula's historic win. Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori hailed Lula's victory in a post on X late Sunday, calling it a "democratic day" for the Brazilian people. Uruguay President Yamandú Orsi congratulated Lula over a call, calling the Brazilian president a "friend."— CNBC's Matthew Tan contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Brazilian stocks rocked as Lula wins presidential election, Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede

title: The arc of Trump: How the president lost the coalition that put him in the White House
description: watch nowPresident Donald Trump forged an extraordinary coalition to win office in 2024, stitching together his base with unusual support from some tr
body: watch nowPresident Donald Trump forged an extraordinary coalition to win office in 2024, stitching together his base with unusual support from some traditional Democratic groups like Hispanics and young people. It was enough to sweep the battleground states and catapult him into office for a second term.The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey shows that coalition is now seriously weakened.Since the beginning of his second term, the president's net approval rating among Latino voters has dropped from -22 to -38, and declined from -28 to -53 among 18- to 34-year olds. Black respondents have moved from -55 to -67.Among all registered voters, his approval has fallen from -7 at the start of his term to -19 in the most recent survey. The decline in the president's approval carries over into the Republican base. Approval from self-described Trump voters has fallen from a net +85 in 2025 to a net of +65. Net approval has even turned negative in the South, from +2 in 2025 to -20 in the latest survey. The results of the latest poll show why Republicans are facing an uphill battle in the midterm elections next week. Trump is not on the ballot — but his presence will be felt. Read the full survey results here.To be sure, Republicans in the survey still give the president an 82% approval rating, and those who say they identify with the MAGA movement are at 90%. But interest in the election is 10 points lower among Republicans than it is for Democrats, and in tight races, the party that better turns out its voters will have an advantage.The survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide found 44% of respondents say their biggest worry if Republicans control Congress is allowing President Trump to operate beyond his constitutional power. By contrast, 28% say their biggest worry for Democratic control is passing policies of Democratic Socialists. For either party's control, registered voters worry that Congress won't do enough to bring down prices.The survey was conducted Oct. 14-18, and was co-led by Democratic pollster Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Public Opinion Strategies. It carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. As a second-term president who had skipped four years between terms, Trump's arc of approval has followed an unusual path. The president left office above water on the economy, with 48% approving and 41% disapproving — high numbers for a president whose last year was overwhelmed by the Covid pandemic.But there was no second-term honeymoon. Trump was immediately underwater in his economic approval rating in the April 2025 CNBC survey. That could have reflected immediate public discontent with the tariff regime and resulting market turmoil. The president's economic approval rating remained negative through most of his first year.The bottom dropped out, however, with the launch of the Iran war. By April 2026, the president's net economic approval rating was plying depths last seen under President Joe Biden amid the aftermath of the pandemic, when the country was facing high inflation and elevated unemployment.In the first quarter of this year, Trump's net economic approval dropped 10 points to -21. It has plunged to -31 in the latest survey. Economic disapproval rose to 65%, the highest for any president CNBC has measured back to President Barack Obama, and one point higher than Biden's worst showing. The survey shows increasing disapproval of Trump's handling of inflation. Over the same time, shooting of Americans by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers began to dominate headlines, eroding support for one of the president's major policy initiatives.The survey this quarter appeared to pick up growing frustration with a host of issues, from immigration to the economy, among those demographic groups that had supported the president in unusual numbers in 2024, with sharp declines in economic and overall approval among Latinos, young people and those in the $50,000 to $75,000 income group.Most ominously for the president, views on the economic outlook fell 22 points for Republicans. Though still net positive, it was the lowest level of economic optimism for Republicans since Biden.These downbeat views on the economy do not automatically translate to votes for Democrats. The survey showed a 7-point preference for Democratic control of Congress, a 3-point gain from the July survey. While Republican economic pessimism grew, so did their preference for a Republican-controlled Congress, from 85% in July to 87% in October.Blue-collar workers show how the president has maintained his base amid growing concern about the economy. Their net economic approval of the president has plunged 22 points to -15 from the beginning of Trump's term to now. But their overall presidential approval remains +6, just a four-point drop. They still prefer a Republican-controlled Congress by 21 points, though that is down from 33 points in July.The days and weeks leading up to the election have seen the president barnstorming through red states, a sign of concern with the base's enthusiasm. But it also creates the possibility that he could fire up his base and bring them out to stanch potential Democratic gains. The survey shows that the extra votes from the coalition that put Trump in the White House in 2024 would be a reach for Republican congressional candidates in 2026.

schema.headline: The arc of Trump: How the president lost the coalition that put him in the White House
